drip.author: brasstacks_barb
drip.title: AITJ for telling someone else's grandkids to get out of the apple trees at the orchard?
drip.body:
Took my two youngest grandchildren apple picking on Sunday. U-pick orchard, lovely cool morning, and a sign at the end of every row asking people not to climb the trees because the branches snap and next year's fruit goes with them.

Two boys, maybe eight and ten, were halfway up a Cortland shaking branches so the apples rained down on the path. Their grandmother was on a bench about thirty feet off, on her phone. After the third apple nearly landed on my granddaughter, I walked over and said, in my classroom voice but not my worst one, "Boys, down please, the trees aren't for climbing." They came down immediately.

The grandmother did not come down at all. She marched over and told me I had no business speaking to her grandchildren when she was right there. I said she was thirty feet away and they were twelve feet up. My grandkids watched the whole exchange, which is the part I keep chewing on. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
comments.body: Not the jerk. The sign did the asking first, you just read it out loud. And apples coming down next to your granddaughter makes it your business, full stop. "I was right there" only counts if right there includes looking up.

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Not the jerk on the what, slightly on the last line. "You were thirty feet away and they were twelve feet up" is a very good sentence, and that's exactly the problem. Once the boys were down, the grown-up part was over. Scoring a point off the grandmother in front of four kids turned a safety thing into a standoff.

replies.author: brasstacks_barb
replies.body: That's fair and I knew it the second it left my mouth. Thirty-one years of not having the last word with parents, and I cashed it all in at an orchard.

comments.author: goalie_mom_deb
comments.body: Not the jerk. Rink rules apply everywhere: if a kid is about to get hurt, or about to hurt mine, any adult in the building gets to say something. Most parents I know are grateful when someone does. The ones who aren't are usually the ones on the bench looking at their phone.

comments.author: twoferone
comments.body: Small dissent from a dad. I'd have gone to the grandmother first. Not because you were wrong, but because a stranger telling my boys off lands differently than a stranger saying "hey, your guys are up the tree." Same result, and she gets to be the one who fixes it.

replies.author: brasstacks_barb
replies.body: With apples dropping beside a small child I don't have thirty feet of diplomacy in me. But for anything less urgent, noted, and you're probably right.

drip.author: sample_size_of_one
drip.title: AITJ for saying the heat stays off until October when my roommate is already cold?
drip.body:
We split the gas bill, and mornings have started dipping to around eight degrees. My roommate wants the heat on. I pointed out that we agreed last year the heat goes on October 1, and that the apartment is sitting at about nineteen inside, which is sweater weather, not hardship.

He says the date was arbitrary, which, fair, I picked it. He also says nineteen in our place feels colder than nineteen because the old windows leak, and he has started wearing a toque indoors in a way I believe is partly theatre. I offered to cover a bigger share of October's bill if he'd hold out two weeks. He said he doesn't want to be paid to be cold.

For the record, I run warm. That may be relevant. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: brasstacks_barb
comments.body: Jerk, gently. You picked the date, you run warm, and you're asking the cold person to prove he's cold. That's three thumbs on one scale. Nineteen with leaky windows is not nineteen. Anyone who taught in a portable classroom in late September can tell you that.

replies.author: sample_size_of_one
replies.body: The portable classroom detail is going to win this for him, isn't it.

comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
comments.body: The date is fine. Calling the toque theatre is the jerk part. Nobody wears a toque indoors for fun. Also, offering someone money to stay cold is a very strange compromise once you sit with it for five seconds.

comments.author: ctrl_z_enjoyer
comments.body: honestly I'm with the date. once the heat goes on in september you've lost october too. but compromise on the thermostat, not the calendar: heat on, set low, and he gets a space heater for his room

replies.author: brasstacks_barb
replies.body: The space heater is the staff-room answer and it's a good one. Nobody has to concede the principle and nobody wears a hat to breakfast.

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Update: the heat is on. Set to nineteen, which the thermostat considers a compromise and my roommate considers a moral victory. He took the toque off within the hour, so I also owe him an apology about the theatre part.

drip.author: DogEaredDarcy
drip.title: Am I the jerk for telling my dad I've heard enough science facts at family dinner?
drip.body:
Some background: my dad famously "doesn't read," and a while back I got him hooked on a big popular-science book. Huge success. He finished it, started it again, and now every family dinner includes at least four facts from it, delivered with the confidence of a man who discovered them personally.

Last weekend he was explaining to my cousin's new girlfriend how many of her atoms probably once belonged to Shakespeare, and I snapped a little. I said "Dad, can we have one dinner that isn't a lecture?" The table went quiet. He laughed it off, but he barely talked for the rest of the meal, and afterward my mom told me he'd been saving that one all week because he was nervous about meeting her.

I turned him into a reader and then told him to stop reading at me. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: brasstacks_barb
comments.body: Jerk, a small one, and you already know it or you wouldn't have written that last line. He wasn't lecturing. He was a nervous man using the one party trick he's proud of, and his own kid took the trick away in front of company. Call him. Ask him for a fact. Mean it.

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Mild jerk, but I'll defend you on one point: four facts per dinner is a real rate, and you're allowed to find it a lot. The problem is only which dinner you picked to say so. In private, next week, framed as "save some for me for when we go for a walk," and nobody goes quiet.

replies.author: DogEaredDarcy
replies.body: "Save some for me" is so much kinder than what I actually said that I'm a little mad about it.

comments.author: chai_and_chapters
comments.body: One book person to another: you got a man who doesn't read to REREAD a science book. Do you know how rare that is? He's not showing off, he's in the honeymoon phase. Don't hand him the hush, hand him the next book. At minimum the facts will rotate.

comments.author: quietkettle
comments.body: Soft jerk. I think the quiet at the table was embarrassment rather than sulking, and embarrassed people forgive easily but are slow to speak up again. Tell him plainly which fact was your favourite. He'll find his voice.

replies.author: DogEaredDarcy
replies.body: Called him this afternoon and asked about the Shakespeare atoms like I'd never heard it. He talked for twenty minutes and then asked what I was reading. We're okay.

drip.author: brasstacks_barb
drip.title: AITJ for telling the neighbour kid I'd rather donate to his school than buy the fundraiser chocolate?
drip.body:
It's that time of year. A boy from down the street, about eleven, rang my bell with an order form: chocolate bars, cookie dough, the works. I told him I don't buy fundraiser chocolate because I end up eating it, which is true, but that I'd happily give twenty dollars straight to his school instead, so they'd keep all of it.

He looked at me like I'd asked him to do long division on the porch. Said he needed "sales" for a prize. I gave him the twenty for the school anyway and he left a bit deflated.

His mother caught me at the mailbox the next day. She said I'd embarrassed him, that the whole point is for kids to practise asking, and that a donation doesn't count toward his prize. At my old school we kept about a dollar a bar. I stand by the math. I'm less sure I stand by the porch. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
comments.body: Not the jerk. The school got more money from you than a whole box of bars would have made them, and you did it without a lecture. Twenty dollars and no chocolate is the better deal for everyone except the prize chart.

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Slight jerk, only because you answered a different question than the one he asked. He's eleven. He wasn't raising funds, he was trying to win a thing. The obvious move is to buy one bar for his count and donate the rest. It costs you one chocolate bar, which I trust you to give away.

replies.author: brasstacks_barb
replies.body: One bar for the count and the rest as a donation. It's so obvious written down that I'm embarrassed I needed a stranger to type it.

comments.author: second_act_sylvia
comments.body: Not the jerk, but I'd knock on his door for a do-over. Tell him you'll buy two bars for his count if he tells you what the prize is. Eleven-year-olds forgive fast when an adult takes their goal seriously.

comments.author: twoferone
comments.body: The mom has a point about the practice, though. Rattling off a pitch to a grown-up at the door is terrifying at eleven, and the reward for getting through it is a sale. Your twenty was generous. It just skipped over the part he'd rehearsed on the sidewalk.

drip.author: DogEaredDarcy
drip.title: Am I the jerk for not trading my window desk to a coworker who dreads the dark months?
drip.body:
I've had the window desk in our corner of the office for four years. I got it because I was there first and nobody else wanted the draft. I love it. I read there on my lunch. It's the only part of the office that feels like mine.

A coworker who started in the spring asked last week, very nicely, if we could swap for the winter. She said the dark months hit her hard and she barely made it to March last year. I said I'd think about it, thought about it, and said no, but offered her the good daylight-bulb desk lamp I bought with my own money.

She said "okay, no worries" and has been perfectly friendly since. But someone else overheard and told me it was cold of me, since it's just a desk and she's clearly struggling. My honest thought was: the winters get to me too, and I never asked anyone for their desk. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Not the jerk. First come, first served, plus an offer of your own lamp, is fair and fairly generous. The coworker who overheard is volunteering your desk, and it's always easy to be generous with someone else's desk.

comments.author: brasstacks_barb
comments.body: Mild jerk, and it's your last line that tips it. "I never asked anyone for their desk" isn't a reason to say no, it's a reason she was brave to ask. There's a middle option you skipped entirely: split the winter. December and January are the worst of it. Give her those two months and keep the rest.

replies.author: DogEaredDarcy
replies.body: Splitting it genuinely never occurred to me, which says something about how tightly I was holding on. Two months I can do.

comments.author: twelve_rescues_later
comments.body: Leaning not the jerk, but if the lamp is the offer, make it a real thing. Set it up at her desk, don't just mention it exists. "I can't give you the window but here's this" can land as a no with a lamp attached, or it can land as someone who noticed. Setting it up is the difference.

drip.author: sample_size_of_one
drip.title: AITJ for skipping my friend's cottage-closing weekend because it's basically unpaid labour with snacks?
drip.body:
A friend of mine has a family cottage, and every year on the last weekend of September she invites a few of us up to "close it." It sounds like a getaway. It is not a getaway. It's hauling the dock out of cold water, dragging the boat up, draining the pipes, and stacking wood, followed by one nice dinner and a sleeping bag on the floor.

I went the last two years. This year I said I'd pass and come up in the summer instead. She said the summer invite is "for people who help close," which, okay, I understand the logic, but I didn't know the summer invite was a subscription.

Another friend in the group says I'm freeloading on past summers. I think two years of dock duty paid for those summers. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: brasstacks_barb
comments.body: Not the jerk for skipping. A little bit the jerk for asking about summer in the same breath. "I won't help close, but pencil me in for a long weekend in August" is the sentence that did it. If you'd just said no thanks, nobody would be keeping a ledger.

replies.author: sample_size_of_one
replies.body: I did say those two things back to back. Lined up like that, it does sound like I was ordering off a menu.

comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
comments.body: Not the jerk. Two years of dragging a dock out of a September lake is a real contribution and you're allowed to retire from it. If an invite comes with a work requirement, the rule should be said up front, not revealed when you decline.

comments.author: solsticegrower
comments.body: Leaning jerk, from someone who spends a weekend every fall putting a big garden to bed with friends. The closing is the price of the summer, and it isn't a hidden price. Everyone who goes up knows why they're there. If you want the summer weekend, haul the dock once more with good grace, then bow out properly next year.

comments.author: ctrl_z_enjoyer
comments.body: not the jerk. "the summer invite is for people who help close" means it was never an invite, it was a shift schedule. you're allowed to not pick up a shift

drip.author: DogEaredDarcy
drip.title: Am I the jerk for putting my pencil-annotated books in the neighbourhood little free library?
drip.body:
There's a little free library box on our corner, looked after by a retired couple who clearly adore it. I've been donating books to it all year. The thing is, I read in pencil. Light underlines, a few notes in the margins, the occasional "!!!" beside a good line.

This week a new laminated sign went up on the box: "Clean copies only please, no marked-up books." Then the husband caught me at the box and said, very politely, that a few people had mentioned it and he'd been pulling mine out. He had them in a tote bag. He handed them back.

I honestly think margin notes are a gift. Finding a stranger's notes in a used book is one of my favourite things in the world. But it's their box. I'm tempted to keep donating them to a different box a few streets over. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Not a jerk for the notes. A jerk if you go through with the other-box plan. He told you the rule to your face and handed your books back. Routing around him is the same donation with a side of sneaky.

replies.author: DogEaredDarcy
replies.body: Said that plainly, it's a lot less charming than it was in my head.

comments.author: brasstacks_barb
comments.body: Not the jerk for loving margin notes. I'd have fought my whole department for your copies. But what's a gift to you is homework to somebody else, and some people open a used book wanting the book, not a reading buddy. Write "annotated, sorry, enjoy" inside the cover and ask the couple whether a labelled shelf would suit them.

comments.author: verdigris
comments.body: Not the jerk in spirit. A stranger's "!!!" in a margin is my favourite kind of found object. But the box has a curator, and the curator has made a curatorial decision. Start your own box. Call it the annotated edition.

drip.author: brasstacks_barb
drip.title: AITJ for picking my neighbour's tomatoes before a frost while she was away?
drip.body:
A frost warning came through on Thursday night. My neighbour, who I'm friendly with but not close to, was away at her sister's for the week. Her tomato plants were loaded, mostly green with a few blushing, and everyone on this street knows what one hard frost does to a tomato plant.

I texted her and got nothing. So I let myself through her side gate, which is never locked, picked everything that was anywhere near full size, and left it all on her porch in paper bags with a note: "Frost warning, saved what I could, lay them on newspaper to ripen. Barb."

The frost never came. Mild night. She got home, found her plants stripped, and was not grateful. She said she'd been counting on another two weeks of them ripening on the vine, and that I had no business in her yard without asking. Am I the jerk?

comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
comments.body: Leaning jerk, knowing your heart was completely in the right place. Going into someone's yard and harvesting their garden is a big move to make on a forecast. An old bedsheet thrown over the plants would have protected them and left the decision to her.

replies.author: brasstacks_barb
replies.body: A bedsheet. I have a linen closet full of them and it did not cross my mind once. I went straight to rescue mode.

comments.author: sample_size_of_one
comments.body: Not the jerk, on the information you had. A frost warning is a forecast of risk, not a promise, and you acted on the downside. It not freezing doesn't make the decision wrong after the fact. That said, she's still allowed to be annoyed. Both things.

comments.author: solsticegrower
comments.body: Gardener's verdict: you picked the full-sized ones, which was the right call. Those will ripen on newspaper just fine. What she lost is two more weeks of vine flavour, and gardeners feel that one in their bones. Bring her a bag of your own ripe ones and I think it blows over.

comments.author: second_act_sylvia
comments.body: Not the jerk, but lead the apology with the text you sent before you went in. She should know you tried to ask. That changes the story from "my neighbour raided my garden" to "my neighbour panicked on my behalf," and the second one is almost sweet.

late_comments.author: DogEaredDarcy
late_comments.body: Came across this reading back through older threads, and it's aged into a warning label for me. A guy with a lucky parking row is just a guy enjoying his morning. Let him have the row. I say this as someone currently working very hard on letting people have their rows.

late_comments.author: brasstacks_barb
late_comments.body: Follow-up for anyone who finds this thread: the text-first system has held. He now texts "kettle?" from the end of my driveway, which is technically a heads-up and technically still an ambush, and I've decided to allow it.

late_comments.author: sample_size_of_one
late_comments.body: Follow-up since people still land on this one: three dinners into the rotation and it's holding. The friend who said I'd corporate-brained our friendship hosted the best one so far, and I didn't say a single word about it, which I think this room would be proud of.
